Sources, Plot, Characters, Commentary
PU draws in an obviously direct way on Aeschylus, in its dramatic conception, and in numer-
ous verbal echoes, particularly in the first act, and to a lesser extent the second act. S. includes an
account of Prometheus in his note to Q Mab viii 211–2, taken from J. F. Newton’s Return to Nature
(see notes to Q Mab in Longman i); but as in his Preface to PU, S.’s explanation of the myth’s mean-
ing in his Q Mab note (where Prometheus is said to ‘represent the human race’) is to be understood
as a gloss on the meaning of the source myth, and not on S.’s own handling of it. PU departs signif-
icantly from its source-myth in Aeschylus, as the Preface makes plain. The action and characters of
Aeschylus’s play are taken from the story of the Titans and the Olympians, as set forth in Hesiod’s
Theogony. In Prometheus Bound, Prometheus, one of the Titans overthrown by the Olympian gods
